cards.explanation: The answer is Fire. The text says the cloud “…appeared like fire above the tabernacle from evening until morning.” I'd have had a hard time sleeping under that one, friends. Daytime, a cloud. Night, a glow.

The answer is False. The text says the cloud “…remained that way continually; the cloud would cover the tabernacle by day, and at night it would appear like fire.” It was there day and night, friends. Some guests leave after one visit, but this cloud stayed around.

The answer is that they set out. Verse 17 says, “Whenever the cloud was lifted from above the Tent, the Israelites would set out…” Cloud goes up, camp gets packed. Packing up a whole camp takes a lot of work, friends, and I can barely close one cookie box without my mustache getting tangled.

The word is settles. The text says, “…wherever the cloud settled, there the Israelites would camp.” The cloud settles, and that's where the camp goes. I'd love it if my own plans were that clear, bakers.

The answer is the LORD's. Going and stopping both came at the LORD's command (Numbers 9:18). Think about that for a second, friends. A whole camp, no schedule on the wall, and they moved when the cloud moved. When my oven timer dings, I still stand there going, "Already?"

The answer is False. Verse 19 says they “…kept the LORD’s charge and did not set out.” Many days of the same view out the tent door, and they stayed anyway. I spent years in the same drawer, so I know about waiting, friends, but they had a cloud to look at.

The answer is that they set out. Verse 21 says, “Whether it was by day or by night, when the cloud was taken up, they would set out.” Night doesn't change anything, friends. I can only imagine the packing in the dark, and I wouldn't trust my mustache with a tent stake.

The answer is True. Verse 23 says, “They camped at the LORD’s command, and they set out at the LORD’s command; they carried out the LORD’s charge according to His command through Moses.” Moses, Israel's leader, was the one it came through, and the people did it. That's the whole picture in one verse, friends.

The answer is calling the people and moving camp. The LORD says to make two trumpets of hammered silver “…to be used for calling the congregation and for having the camps set out.” Two jobs for two trumpets, friends. That's better than my old drawer, where nothing had a job at all.

The answer is False. Verse 3 says, “When both are sounded, the whole congregation is to assemble before you at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Only one trumpet gathers the leaders (Numbers 10:4). Two trumpets, whole crowd, friends.

The word is heads. Verse 4 says, “…then the leaders, the heads of the clans of Israel, are to gather before you.” One trumpet gets the leaders, and two get everybody. Simple system, and I like simple, bakers. My bakery has one oven mitt and I still lose it.

The answer is True. Verse 6 says, “When you sound the short blasts a second time, the camps that lie on the south side are to set out.” The first short blasts are for the camps on the east side (Numbers 10:5). The second time, it's the south side. Two rounds of short blasts, two sets of camps, friends.

The answer is gathering the assembly. Verse 7 says, “To convene the assembly, you are to sound long blasts, not short ones.” Short is for setting out, and long is for gathering. Mix them up, friends, and I'd be standing around holding a tent stake.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “When you enter into battle in your land against an adversary who attacks you, sound short blasts on the trumpets, and you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved from your enemies.” (Numbers 10:9). Notice the setting, friends. It's battle in their land, against an adversary who attacks them. And the promise is the LORD's own word.

The word is reminder. The trumpets are to be blown “…to serve as a reminder for you before your God.” The command covers joyous occasions, appointed feasts and the beginning of each month. That beats a sticky note on the fridge by a mile, bakers.
